Such indeed is this shitty world.”
As he turned his steed's head,
While he stood weeping in sorrow,
“This Talas that quenches my longing,
My companion, gray-maned Manas.
This gray-maned hero took a migration from Keng-Kol,
And every place he encountered has a vengeance to exact.
These sheikhs with courts and costly riding boots,
The multitude of Kokand and Marghilan,
These western people have a vengeance to exact.
“Before I reach her, may Kanykey
Not scatter her travel provisions.
That bondwoman born to sorrow,
May she not flee farther west.
Of those Six Cities and Kokand,
May hunters coming upon her,
Saying, ‘She is a fugitive woman,’
Not seize my little one!
May they not cut off his head in the wilderness,
May they not leave my fire extinguished!
Or if this thought of mine proves false—
If those six scoundrels should overtake her,
May they not attack the widow
Where she lies within her cave;
Beating the widow in the open,
May they not suddenly spill her blood like a steel blade!
Or, crushing those ladies,
May they not carry off my orphan!
Those six foul-looking scoundrels,
May they not together bring about my ruin!”
Then Bakay the leopard
Hurriedly saddled his horse,
Fearing for his orphan.
The white bridle tied with rounded knots,
While my mighty Manas was alive,
Had he not made it to match?
A bridle fitting Taytoru.
“God grant success!” he said, without delay.
Your mountain-like elder Bakay,
Taking the saddle Zhamgyrchy had given,
Now Bakay rejoiced.
Let me tell of the saddle:
Ak-Kangky, made by Almambet—
Both sides were broad plates of iron,
The front bow was yellow gold,
The rear bow was pure silver.
Set upon the swift steed, it would not gall him,
Even on a journey of six months,
It would never make a single place sore.
Remaking it and stitching it together,
“When he sets out for Beijing,
Let him keep it as a gift,” he said,
Entrusting it to the warrior Semetey.
The terrible things that were to happen,
Had he not known before he went?
That Semetey would wander in exile,
Had he not foreseen before he went!
Gray-maned Alman the leopard,
To Zhamgyrchy of the Eshteks,
Entrusted Ak-Kangky;
Had he not given it before he went?
A leather underpad and a blue saddlecloth,
Preparing them for Taytoru,
The hero Bakay saddled him without hesitation.
“For six months he has roamed,
Not once touched by a switch,
Ridden by nothing but flies.
This sturdy racer Taytoru,
When he comes into her hands,
Will my widow ride away on him?
Lashing him this way and that,
Kicking him on the right and left,
Will he be afflicted with mange?
Will he earn a bad name,
Will the bay become a cripple?”
Khan Bakay grieved.
When he felt the flesh along the mane,
The horse was fit to ride upon a journey;
Every fiber of his flesh was in condition.
Then Bakay thought:
“Gray-maned Manas, favored by Kyzyr,
Truly has a mighty spirit.”
Mustering himself to go to the orphan,
Bakay's heart was deeply moved.
Then Bakay the leopard,
His gray steed beneath him,
Whipped him this way and that,
Turning aside and taking shortcuts,
Leading Taytoru,
As he came up straight ahead,
God granted his wish.
Breaking courts and taking booty,
Bearing the name of Manas the Mighty,
When he dealt slaughter to the Chinese,
He was sixteen years of age.
Toward Beijing of the khakan,
Driving the Chinese in rout,
When your hero pursued them toward Beijing,
Five khojas barred his way.
“Even the four companions cannot reach Beijing;
You have not the strength—stop!” they said.
The Caliph, khan of Mecca,
When he took hold of Manas,
A star stirred in the sky.
Becoming friends for the world beyond,
A gray one from among white horses,
Becoming friends for the afterlife,
Holding the lead rope and sobbing,
Entrusting him earnestly, crying aloud,
That khoja, the manifest sovereign,
Gave Akborchuk into his keeping.
“My mother Chyyyrdy, blessed with support,
Will know that he is a child,” he said.
“My poor old mother
Shall have him as her own to ride,” he said.
That Akborchuk of Chyyyrdy's
Was indeed a beast Manas had given,
To his unfortunate mother,
Assigned as her own.
In Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
While the Kyrgyz lay at ease,
Twilight came and the sun set;
The people lay utterly still.
To great Zhakyp's court,
To the dark eye of the spring,
To Khan Zhakyp himself,
Skimming the earth, Bakay the leopard
Came in alone.
Before the stars had parted,
In the moon's darkness,
Unseen by a single soul.
When the dogs divided the court,
When your mighty Manas died,
Akborchuk had fled, frisking,
And had been taken as booty.
Akborchuk, standing at the tethering rail,
Broke his halter and escaped;
Now he had come frisking to Bakay.
The wind could not catch his trot;
He was a beast like an unseen spirit.
Watching over livestock morning and night,
The grandfather—that swine of a khan—
Zhakyp's saddle was upon him.
Then his neck, like a wild ram's,
Akborchuk turned toward him.
Meeting in broad Talas,
Before stately Bakay,
Akborchuk stood still.
Then Bakay rejoiced:
“In six journeys I have made,
Was there a night like the Night of Power?
This too is a sacred omen.
Will there be a day when I see my orphan?”
Then Bakay—Khojosan—
Took two fat horses,
Took two skins of milk,
And galloped down Talas,
Racing down Keng-Kol,
Akborchuk and Taytoru,
Leading them toward the lady,
Bakay traveled without stopping,
Unable to rest, riding through the night.
Stars shot through the sky,
Hurrying toward the qibla.
Stars trembled overhead,
Moving one by one toward the qibla.
Dawn brightened and swelled,
Dawn split open, swelling forth.
Ah, father, the dawn broke clear;
The Balance stars had set.
As the still dawn advanced,
As light fell upon the earth,
At Kara-Tash of Kayyp-Kyr,
With wild rams and ibex mingled on its slopes,
In the hollow of Chalkandy,
Then Bakay the leopard
Lay down and slept his fill.
He let the steeds graze.
At the clear water of a crossing spring,
He let them quench their thirst.
The snuff in his tobacco box,
Extending his fingers, he took a pinch,
And put it against his palate.
Khan Bakay then spoke his sorrow.
“This Kara-Üngkür standing here
Is the very cave where treasure was gathered.
Tears flow without stopping from my eyes.
While Khan Manas was alive,
Gold and silver lay mingled.
It has become a stone that holds my gold,
Since my precious one's eyes closed in death.
The six scoundrels have become the people's chiefs.
There you lie—farewell,
My cave where treasure was gathered!
Those who guarded my cave,
With Khan Bölökböy at their head,
Where have they gone, the noble ones,
My forty-one guards.”
Bakay leaned upon his battle-axe,
Girding his waist firmly,
He called aloud, “Bölökbay!”
“They must have plundered my gold,
And that poor Bölökbay,
They must have cleaved him on the road.
Together they have brought my ruin.
O God, they must have slaughtered my forty-one!”
Khan Bakay wept and wailed,
Standing there, adding words to his lament.
Then the lame smith Bölökbay
Heard the prince's voice.
From Zhar-Kyya of Zhangyryk,
They were coming down,
With the hero Bölökbay at their head.
There, in a line one horse wide,
When the dogs assaulted the court,
Laying hands upon the treasury,
Drawing their bows like falling rain,
When the dogs rushed in together,
The treasure cave became a mountain,
The six scoundrels and forty companions,
All the Kyrgyz gathered together,
Became Bölökbay's enemies.
Because of the treasury,
They drew their bows like falling rain,
Firing missiles like hail,
Tormenting Bölökbay,
Forcing their way into Manas's treasury.
Then the lame smith Bölökbay,
Refusing to obey their words,
Refusing to give up the treasure,
For seven days in their midst,
Bölökbay had held out,
Taking wounds in seventy places.
The forty guards came out shooting,
For six days amid the fighting,
The poor men were at their wits' end,
Taking wounds in sixty places.
Their four kinds of livestock scattered,
Overwhelmed from above,
Their star darkened in the sky.
After twelve days of shooting,
Bölökbay broke free and escaped.
Abyke, Köbösh—the six scoundrels—
Were not content with the gold.
“I shall catch Bölökbay and butcher him,
I shall gouge out his eyes,
I shall seize him and crush him,” they said.
They tracked his every trace,
Pursuing him till they turned pale,
As though he had slaughtered seven generations of their fathers,
When they pursued him relentlessly,
With their marksmen crouching,
Sending them ahead,
The most skillful of their spearmen,
Their lances thrusting high,
